records.name_note: NC State and RHS both have readable dedicated pages for this exact taxon, and they use different lead names. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and in the same order as its page-title parenthetical: it opens with Annual Milkweed, includes Blood Flower and Swallow Wort, and ends with Tropical Milkweed; the page's Description prose opens with the sentence naming Tropical Milkweed, which is the name used here. RHS's page title gives the common name bloodflower, and its Other common names line does not include tropical milkweed.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries two separate pieces of toxicity evidence. (1) Tags and Problems field: the page's toxicity tags are #poisonous, #problem for horses, #problem for dogs and #problem for cats; the Problems field lists Messy, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. The cat, dog and horse tags carry no severity, symptom list or plant-part detail of their own. Plant Type is rendered as Annual and Poisonous. (2) The "Poisonous to Humans" block, which is human-scoped: Poison Severity: Low (the page also says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."). Poison Symptoms: "Can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weakness, lethargy, and confusion if eaten in quantity. Milky sap can cause contact dermatitis and eye irritation". Poison Toxic Principle: Cardiac glycosides and resinoids. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. The Low severity rating comes from the Poisonous to Humans / Poison Severity heading, not from the cat, dog or horse tags. Handling warning: "Milky sap can cause contact dermatitis and eye irritation" (the description says the leaves and stems have a milky juice when damaged). RHS's dedicated page, under Potentially harmful, says "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling"; it names no animal and gives no severity, symptoms or plant parts, so it does not bear on the cat and dog tags.

MoBot's dedicated Plant Finder page (taxonid=276911, served from plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be loaded because its TLS certificate fails verification from this machine. UF/IFAS's dedicated fact sheet FPS-49 (edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/fp049) redirects to ask.ifas.ufl.edu and returns HTTP 410 ("The publication you requested is no longer available on Ask IFAS."). Clemson HGIC returned a 403 bot block. Nothing was borrowed from the unreadable sources or from the other Asclepias records.

Monarch advice, exactly as NC State states it: 'Although milkweed is an important food source for the Monarch butterfly caterpillar, this plant isn't recommended for attracting Monarch Butterflies because they can bloom out of sync with Monarch migration patterns and hold them too long in one area, affecting their populations.  Plant one of the native milkweeds instead.' And: 'Ophryocystis elektroscirrha a monarch parasite can occur on this plant in locations where this plant does not die back in the winter months.' NC State adds that cutting the plant down will help remediate this but the best course is to plant a native milkweed instead. NC State's native alternatives listed on the page: Asclepias incarnata, A. syriaca, A. tuberosa, A. variegata.

Swallow Wort is one of the Common Name(s) NC State lists for this species; the same name is also used for the invasive Vincetoxicum swallow-worts, so it should not be used as a lookup key (no admissible source cited for that second use, so it is noted here, not in name_note).

is_houseplant is false (set at landing): NC State's Landscape Location field lists Container, Meadow, Naturalized Area, Patio, Slope/Bank, Vertical Spaces and Walkways, with no Houseplants value, and its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field reads 8a-11b; RHS suggests Sub-tropical and Patio and container plants. No admissible source frames it as a houseplant.

toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags (scoped to cats and dogs). There is no symptom or severity detail for pets; the Low severity and symptom list are human-scoped. Problem for Horses is also tagged.

is_edible false rests on NC State's Poisonous to Humans block (Poison Symptoms "Can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weakness, lethargy, and confusion if eaten in quantity.", Poison Severity Low) and on RHS's Potentially harmful field ("Harmful if eaten."); no admissible source states that any part of this plant is used for food. NC State's Poison Part list includes Bark; NC State calls the plant a tender erect perennial and RHS calls it an upright evergreen sub-shrub, so the list is kept as rendered.

soil_ph_min is null: NC State lists Soil pH as Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the Acid band is open-ended (no floor). soil_ph_max is 8, the closed top of NC State's Neutral band, set at landing: RHS's pH field reads Acid or Neutral and lists no Alkaline value, so it does not rule out that ceiling (the check the audit said passes).

soil_drainage moderate: Good Drainage (structured field) plus #wet soils tolerant and #dry soils tolerant tags plus 'moist, fertile, well-drained soil' in the prose; not fast, not moisture_retentive. RHS's Moisture field reads Well–drained alone, which does not decide the band.

water_regime and all watering/fertilizing fields left null: NC State gives no watering or feeding statement for this species, only soil adjectives and wet/dry-soil tolerance tags. Chill damage, temperatures, humidity and indoor light left null for lack of admissible species-specific figures; the tag #frost tender and 'It will remain as an evergreen to Zone 9b' are not an onset temperature.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure is inside NC State's generic light-category legend ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'), not species prose, and it is a minimum, not a maximum.

soil_base garden_bed taken from NC State's in-ground planting statement; NC State's Landscape Location also lists Container and Patio, so container culture is possible but no potting-mix guidance is given.

records.name_note: NC State's page for this exact taxon carries a Common Name(s) list that is alphabetized and reads Forget-me-not then Woodland Forget-Me-Not; the page-title parenthetical renders the same two names in the same order. The body prose, however, refers to the plant as Woodland Forget-Me-Not from its first sentence. The sources split: RHS's dedicated page leads with garden forget-me-not and lists wood forget-me-not under Other common names. The bare Forget-me-not is also the first name NC State lists for Myosotis scorpioides, so common_name uses the specific Woodland Forget-Me-Not, the name NC State's prose leads with.
unknowns: Every field value in this record rests on NC State's dedicated page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/myosotis-sylvatica/); RHS is cited for the accepted name, the name split and drainage. RHS does have a dedicated page for this exact taxon, https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/41558/myosotis-sylvatica/details (the slug first guessed missed it). It gives Name Status Correct, the common name garden forget-me-not (Other common names: wood forget-me-not, ysgorpionllys y coed), Position Partial shade, Moisture Moist but well-drained, pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres, hardiness H6, and the Plants for pollinators badge. MoBot's dedicated page, https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=278005, redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org, whose certificate chain fails verification from this machine; as read by the auditor in a browser (not cited: the page refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it) it gives Common Name woodland forget-me-not, Sun Full sun to part shade, Water Medium, Height 0.50 to 1.00 feet, Spread 0.50 to 0.75 feet, Zone 3 to 8, and the notice Midwest Noxious Weed: Do Not Plant. The Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA pages were not found or not loadable.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: NC State carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for this page, and no admissible page naming cats or dogs was found.

is_edible is null: no admissible source addresses eating this plant. is_houseplant is false (set at landing): NC State's Landscape Location field lists Naturalized Area, Pond, Slope/Bank and Woodland, with no Houseplants value, and the page treats it as a garden plant; no admissible source frames it as a houseplant.

Noxious-weed status, quoted exactly from NC State: "Woodland Forget-Me-Not is listed as a noxious weed in one or more Midwestern states." The page's Problems field also lists Short-lived and Weedy. Self-seeding habit, exactly as worded: "plants will persist in the garden for many years by freely and sometimes aggressively self-seeding." NC State suggests deadheading to prevent excessive seeding.

Life cycle as stated by NC State: the structured Life Cycle field renders three values (Annual, Biennial, Perennial) and the Plant Type field renders four (Annual, Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Wildflower, followed by a separate Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics label). The prose calls it a spring flowering herbaceous perennial often grown as an annual and, separately, a short-lived perennial that is best grown as an annual, which can also be grown as a biennial.

soil_drainage is moderate, not moisture_retentive: NC State's Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Wet; the prose says consistently moist, well-drained soils is what the plant does well in (a preference), and that shallow standing water is tolerated. #wet soils tolerant rules out fast. No admissible page makes moist soil a cultivation requirement.

water_regime keep_moist rests on the single watering condition that the plant adapts to garden soil of loam or clay-loam "if it is kept sufficiently moist". It is a one-source, conditional statement; NC State gives no watering schedule, interval, dry-down target or check depth, so those fields are null. The structured Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Wet) is a mild counterpoint that does not call for constant wetness, and MoBot's structured Water field reads Medium (not cited: the page refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it), a mid-scale rating that does not itself support keep_moist.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, mapped to full_sun and part_shade; the prose says full sun to part shade with some afternoon shade appreciated in hot summer climates. RHS's Position field lists Partial shade only, so RHS dissents on full_sun, which rests on NC State's Light field and prose. MoBot's Sun field reads Full sun to part shade (not cited: the page refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it). direct_sun_hours_max is null because the hour ranges appear only in the site-wide light-category legend text, not in species-specific prose.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer and chill-damage onset are not stated by any admissible page found; all left null. NC State gives no soil pH, and RHS's pH field reads Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, which sets no numeric floor or ceiling, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max stay null. NC State's USDA hardiness zone range (3a-8b), MoBot's Zone 3 to 8 and RHS's H6 rating are survival ratings, not chill-damage figures.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in come from NC State's species-level Dimensions block (Height 0 ft 6 in to 1 ft 0 in; Width 0 ft 6 in to 0 ft 10 in), converted to inches. Cultivar sizes on the page (for example 'Victoria Blue' to 6-8 inches) were not used.
soil_base garden_bed is inferred only from the page treating this as an in-ground wildflower/border plant adapting to garden soil; no source gives a potting-mix recommendation.

RHS's dedicated page leads with heart's ease in both its page title and its plant-profile subtitle, and its separate Other common names field lists 45 names, among them Johnny-jump-up, pansy and wild pansy. NC State's dedicated page has the bare binomial as its H1 and its Description opens with Wild pansy; its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, opens with Come-and-Cuddle-Me, and includes Heartsease, Heart's Ease, Johnny Jump Up, Johnny Jump-Up, Johnny-Jump Up, Pansy and Wild Pansy. Johnny Jump-Up leads neither page; Clemson HGIC's factsheet puts Viola cornuta and Viola tricolor under one heading, Johnny-Jump-Ups, and NC State's Viola rafinesquei page also lists Johnny Jump-Up. NC State says this species is the parent plant of modern pansy hybrids; plain Pansy is the common name of the separately landed Viola × wittrockiana, whose NC State Common Name(s) list reads Lady's Delight and Pansy. Heart's Ease is used as the common name: it is RHS's lead in both its page title and its subtitle, and NC State lists it as both Heartsease and Heart's Ease.
records.toxicity_detail: Edibility only; no pet or human toxicity is stated. NC State's structured Edibility line says "Flowers are edible and have a slight minty flavor." Its prose says "The beautiful flowers are edible in small amounts but have little flavor." The two statements conflict on flavor (slight minty vs. little flavor); the condition is that the flowers are edible in small amounts only. The page's Plant Type values are Annual, Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Wildflower. NC State's page carries no poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag, and no admissible page checked names cats or dogs, so pet toxicity is unrecorded.

records.toxicity_detail: Sources: NC State and RHS. NC State Tags: #problem for children #problem for dogs #poisonous #problem for cats (also #contact dermatitis, #poisonous if ingested, #weedy); the structured Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Weedy. Plant Type values: Annual, Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Weed. The page says 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics', and its Poison Severity 'Low' sits in the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' block; the Problem-for-Cats/Dogs/Children tags are separate and carry no severity rating. Poison Symptoms: 'The milky white latex sap found in all plant parts can cause mild to severe contact dermatitis. If contact with the eyes occurs the sap can cause temporary to permanent damage to the cornea. If eaten, blistering can occur on lips and oral mucosa. Avoid ingesting plant parts and keep plants away from pets and children.' Poison Toxic Principle: Diterpene esters in milky latex. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (structured, full list): Flowers, Leaves, Sap/Juice, Stems; the symptoms text, by contrast, puts the latex sap in all plant parts. Description prose: 'As with most euphorbias, the stems and leaves contains a milky sap that is a skin and eye irritant.' and 'Graceful spurge is toxic if ingested. Keep out of the reach of small children and pets. Wear protective gloves when handling this plant since the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant.' RHS's dedicated profile agrees: its Potentially harmful row reads 'Humans/Pets: IRRITANT to skin/eye; harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants', naming no plant part, no severity and no particular animal. The two sources do not disagree on scope or edibility.
unknowns: Every value here rests on NC State's dedicated species page. Two more admissible dedicated pages load from this machine: RHS's profile (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/176926/euphorbia-hypericifolia/details) and UF/IFAS's EDIS publication EP522 (https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/EP522), a weed-management publication for ornamental crop production. RHS agrees with the sun, drainage, toxicity and edibility values (Position 'Full sun, Partial shade'; Moisture 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'; its Potentially harmful row, quoted in toxicity_detail). It gives pH as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (no bound) and hardiness H2 (a rating, not a damage-onset temperature), and it renders no common name and no pollinator badge. The pages disagree on size: RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread as '0.1-0.5 metres' (3.9-19.7 in) and describes 'stems to 60cm (2ft) high and wide', and EP522 says 'Graceful sandmat can grow over 2 ft tall but normally grows to less than 1 ft tall.' NC State's Dimensions block stays the anchor because the species has its own NC State page. EP522 gives no toxicity, watering, soil or fertilizer guidance. MoBot's Plant Finder did not load from this machine.

Invasive-where-introduced wording as stated: 'This plant can spread invasively, particularly in places where it has been introduced such as the Pacific Islands.' soil_drainage is moderate. RHS's dedicated profile gives Moisture as 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'. NC State says 'It requires well-drained soils and is poor soils tolerant.', and its Soil Drainage field renders Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, which is not sharp or sandy drainage. NC State's Soil Texture values include Sand, and its prose says 'It is also deer, rabbit, dry soil, drought, and air pollution tolerant.', so a fast reading is arguable. Neither page describes wet tolerance in cultivation. NC State's 'Overwatering can be lethal to the plant.' is a watering caution, not a drainage value.

water_regime is null because no admissible page gives a watering instruction. NC State's only watering-related text is the caution 'Overwatering can be lethal to the plant.' in its Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems paragraph. It does not say how far the soil should dry between waterings. NC State's dry-soil and drought tolerance is a trait, not a regime. RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well–drained or Well–drained') is a drainage descriptor, and UF/IFAS's EP522 gives no watering guidance. The interval, dry-down and check-depth fields are null.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's page title parenthetical lists the common names alphabetically (Elfin Herb, False Heather, Hawaiian Heather, Hyssop-Leaf Waxweed, Mexican Heather), and its Common Name(s) list renders the same five names in the same order, so Elfin Herb comes first; the page's Description opens with Mexican heather, and Mexican Heather is used as the common name. RHS's page title pairs the binomial with false heather, and its Other common names line reads elfin herb. False Heather is kept as an alternate: NC State says that although Mexican heather resembles heather, it is not a member of the heather family, hence the common name false heather. NC State's 'Previously known as' list includes Cuphea rivularis and Parsonsia hyssopifolia (among other former names). No field is taken from C. ignea, C. llavea or any cultivar page.
unknowns: NC State and RHS were read. RHS's dedicated profile for the species (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/5036/cuphea-hyssopifolia/details) gives page title 'Cuphea hyssopifolia | false heather', Other common names 'elfin herb', Name Status 'Correct', and plant types Bedding, Conservatory Greenhouse, Houseplants and Shrubs. Its Position is 'Full sun, Partial shade'; part_shade is left out of outdoor_sun_exposure because NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun only. Soil Types are Chalk, Loam and Sand, and Moisture is a bare 'Well–drained'. Its pH field, 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', disagrees with NC State's open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)', so soil pH stays null. Hardiness is 'H2', a rating rather than a damage-onset temperature. Max Height is '0.1-0.5 metres' (3.9-19.7 in) and Max Spread '0.5-1 metres' (19.7-39.4 in), and its description says 'A compact, bushy spreading evergreen shrub to 45cm in height' (about 17.7 in). That is shorter than NC State's Dimensions height of 12-24 in, which stays the size anchor. RHS has no toxicity or harm field, no pet line, no edibility statement and no pollinator tag. Its Cultivation text, 'Best grown in well-drained soil in a sheltered site in sun or partial shade but shade from hot sun. Alternatively grow in a pot under glass or as a houseplant', is word-for-word the text on RHS's Cuphea ignea page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/5037/cuphea-ignea/details), so it is genus boilerplate and supports no field. The Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS and Clemson pages for this species would not load or were not found (connection failure, 404, 403), so they are not cross-checked.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: NC State carries no poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for this species. Its Ethnobotany line (leaves and flowers used as a tonic and for fevers and coughs, and as an insecticide) is not a toxicity statement.
is_edible is null: no admissible page addresses eating the plant as food.

is_houseplant is true: NC State's Landscape Location field lists Container, Hanging Baskets, Houseplants, Patio and Walkways, its prose says 'In cooler climates, it is usually grown as a perennial container plant or houseplant.' and 'If grown indoors, place the plant in a warm, sunny location.', and it advises monitoring for pests 'particularly on indoor plants'; RHS types the species Bedding, Conservatory Greenhouse, Houseplants and Shrubs. The same NC State page says 'In the garden, it is typically grown as an annual.' and 'In our climate, Mexican heather can be used as an annual.' RHS's Cultivation sentence ending 'or as a houseplant' is not used, because the identical sentence appears on RHS's Cuphea ignea page and is genus boilerplate. NC State's Dimensions figures are under 120 in, so the houseplant size rule leaves the size fields as they are.

Life cycle and hardiness as NC State states them: the structured Life Cycle field lists both Annual and Perennial (not Annual alone), Plant Type lists Annual, Ground Cover, Perennial and Shrub, and the prose calls it a dense evergreen shrub. The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field reads 9a to 11b, while the prose says it dies back to the ground in Zones 8 to 9 and will sprout from the base if well mulched. In its climate NC State says it can be used as an annual. A hardiness zone is not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.
Soil pH is null: NC State's only pH value is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)', which gives no floor or ceiling.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's Soil Drainage tags 'Good Drainage', 'Moist' and 'Occasionally Dry' plus the prose 'adaptable to various soils with good drainage'. The tags do not include any wet-tolerance value.

water_regime is keep_moist from the prose preference 'grows best with regular moisture'. Counterpoint on the same page: it also 'withstands high summer heat and some drought' and carries a 'drought tolerant' tag. NC State states no watering schedule, so all day-interval and dry-down fields are null.

soil_base is garden_bed because NC State describes in-ground landscape use (border, groundcover, mass planting) with a Soil Texture field of Clay, Loam (Silt) and Sand. It also describes container and hanging-basket use, with no potting-mix guidance.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figure is in NC State's site-wide Light legend 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', which is not species prose. The structured Light field is Full sun only.

Humidity, indoor light (foot-candles), day and night temperature ranges and fertilizer are not stated for this species on NC State or RHS. NC State's humidity evidence is tolerance only, the '#humidity tolerant' tag and Humidity among its Resistance To Challenges values (Heat, Humidity, Salt), and neither is a humidity need.
Mature size: NC State's Dimensions block gives Height 1 ft 0 in to 2 ft 0 in (12 to 24 in) and Width 0 ft 9 in to 2 ft 8 in (9 to 32 in); its prose says it grows up to 2 feet tall and wide.

records.name_note: The admissible dedicated pages split on the lead name. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list for Matthiola incana is alphabetized, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, and reads Brompton Stock, Gillyflower, Stock, Stocks, Ten Weeks Stock; its Description prose opens with Stock. RHS renders Brompton stock beneath its H1 (page title 'Matthiola incana | Brompton stock'), lists cluster-leaved stock, common stock, gilliflower, hoary stock, hopes, queen's stock and wallflower stock as other common names, and gives Matthiola incana 'Brompton' as a synonym. NC State says 'A number of Stock varieties have been developed, mostly hybrids involving M. incana, M. sinuata and M. odorata, to the point where strict species plants are no longer available.' No field was taken from M. longipetala or any series or cultivar page. Brompton Stock is landed as the first name of NC State's list and the lead of RHS's page title and subtitle.
unknowns: Three admissible dedicated pages exist for Matthiola incana: NC State Plant Toolbox (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/matthiola-incana/), RHS (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/48284/matthiola-incana/details) and Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=278041, which refuses non-browser clients from this machine, so nothing rests on it: not cited: the page refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it). RHS and MoBot were read after the research pass (2026-10-07). Both agree with NC State on size (MoBot Height 1.00 to 3.00 feet and Spread 0.75 to 1.50 feet; RHS Max Height 0.5-1 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres), and RHS agrees on drainage (Moist but well-drained), pH (Alkaline or Neutral) and pollinators (Plants for pollinators). Both list full sun only. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium', which under this catalog's rules never supports keep_moist, so water_regime stays null. MoBot's Common Name field reads brompton stock, and its prose says the name brompton stock 'is still used today, often in general terms, for stock plants.' No dedicated Clemson HGIC page was found.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: NC State carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag on this page, and no admissible page naming cats or dogs was found, so toxic_to_pets is null (not false).
is_edible is null: no admissible page addresses eating this plant.

day_f_max 80 comes from NC State's statement that plants begin to decline in the summer when temperatures are above 80 F. NC State does not say day or night, but Missouri Botanical Garden (not cited: the page refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it) frames the same limit as daytime: 'Plants generally decline by early to mid-summer once daytime summer temperatures in the 80s or higher become common.' NC State says the plants also suffer from hot night-time conditions, and MoBot that they dislike hot nighttime conditions. Neither gives a night temperature, so night_f_max is null. chill_damage_f is null because no admissible page states a cold-damage onset; RHS's H4 rating and MoBot's Zone 7 to 10 are survival ratings, not onsets.

soil_ph_min 6.0 is the floor of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band, the lowest band the page lists; the page also says it will not do well in acidic soil. soil_ph_max is null because NC State also lists Alkaline (>8.0), which is open-ended.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair; the 'consistently moist, well-drained soils' clause is a soil preference, not a watering instruction, and not a moisture_retentive requirement.
water_regime and the watering interval fields are null: NC State gives no watering statement, only soil adjectives and the Moist drainage tag.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), but its prose says only that it does tolerate some light shade. RHS's Position field lists Full sun only, and Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads 'Sun: Full sun', with prose saying 'Plants tolerate some light shade.' (not cited: the page refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it). part_shade is therefore not landed.

soil_base garden_bed rests on NC State's soil prose and its Design Feature field (Border, Mass Planting); NC State also lists Container, Patio and Small Space under Landscape Location, and RHS lists Patio and container plants among its suggested locations.

is_houseplant is false (set at landing): NC State's Landscape Location field lists Container, Patio and Small Space, with no Houseplants value, and NC State describes it as a cool-season plant best used as an annual in the south; no admissible source frames it as a houseplant.
No light foot-candle, humidity, fertilizer or temperature range data was found on the admissible pages.

Size is from NC State's Dimensions block (1 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. tall, 0 ft. 9 in. - 1 ft. 6 in. wide), converted to inches; NC State's prose gives a mature height of 3 feet, consistent with the upper bound.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b101 (annuals, bedding and container plants) landed from the post-audit records, continuing a half-written repair script left by an earlier landing agent (its Tropical Milkweed block kept, plus NC State's whole Poison block quoted as the page's contiguous label/value run). Auditor-supplied corrected wording used verbatim except where it rested on Missouri Botanical Garden, which refuses this machine and is not cached (standing rule 4: those sentences move to unknowns, marked not cited). Every added or changed quote was checked against the shared page cache through verify_quotes' own fetch+extract before it was applied; no auditor-proposed 'Woody Plant' Plant Type value was used. Landing decisions: Viola tricolor lands as Heart's Ease (RHS's page-title and subtitle lead, listed twice by NC State; no dedicated page leads with the researched Johnny Jump-Up, which Clemson files under V. cornuta too), kept distinct from b14's Pansy (Viola × wittrockiana); Matthiola incana lands as Brompton Stock (NC State's first list item matching its title parenthetical, RHS's subtitle and title) instead of the researched Stock; Stock drops part_shade (NC State prose makes shade a tolerance, RHS Position Full sun only, MoBot Sun Full sun per the auditor); Heliotrope's seven MoBot citations dropped, its is_houseplant re-rested on NC State's Landscape Location Houseplants value and cool_rest_note nulled (MoBot alone); Mexican Heather is_houseplant set true on the audit's NC State and RHS evidence; Heliotrope is_edible set false; Tropical Milkweed soil_ph_max 8 (RHS lists no alkaline soils); is_houseplant set false on the other six from NC State's Landscape Location fields; water_regime refuted to null for Heart's Ease and Graceful Spurge.
